analysis.one_liner: Requires a nationwide government survey to find where toxic PFAS chemicals have contaminated America's water and soil.
analysis.headline: The bill to map PFAS 'forever chemicals' in America's water nationwide passed no chamber and died in a House committee after a single hearing.
analysis.plain_summary: PFAS "forever chemicals" — used in nonstick pans, waterproof clothing, food packaging, and firefighting foam — can cause health problems, and there was no consistent national picture of where they had ended up in water supplies. This bill would have directed the U.S. Geological Survey to set a standard way to detect these chemicals and then test lakes, rivers, wells, aquifers, and soil across the country, starting at drinking water sources near known contamination. The results would be handed to the EPA and state regulators to guide cleanup priorities. It never received a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who drinks water, but especially communities near military bases, airports, factories, or other sites where PFAS-laden firefighting foam or industrial waste has leaked. The bill prioritized testing drinking water sources near known or suspected PFAS releases, and its data would have helped regulators decide where cleanup matters most. States and local health officials would also get consistent, high-quality detection data they currently lack.

how_it_helps.text: It directs the U.S. Geological Survey to establish a standard method for detecting PFAS and then sample lakes, rivers, wells, aquifers, and soil across the country.
It requires testing to start at drinking water sources near known or suspected PFAS releases, measured before any water treatment, with direct human exposure through drinking water as the priority.

It requires the results be given to the EPA and state regulators and used to guide health-impact assessments and cleanup priorities, and it authorizes $5 million for 2020 and $10 million per year for 2021-2024 to do the work.

analysis.who_pays: Chemical manufacturers and industrial users of PFAS — companies making nonstick cookware, waterproof clothing, stain-resistant fabrics, food packaging, and firefighting foam — would face a national map showing where their products' chemicals have spread, which could strengthen future regulation and cleanup liability. They pay nothing directly under the bill, which authorizes only federal spending.

drawbacks.text: The bill only measures the problem, it does not fix it: the data would inform exposure assessments and 'remediation priorities,' but the bill sets no cleanup requirements, no drinking-water limits, and no new restrictions on PFAS manufacturers.

It authorizes up to roughly $10 million per year in federal spending, a modest cost but a real one, and the survey could overlap with sampling states and other agencies already do; the bill directs the USGS to coordinate with states and the EPA to avoid unnecessary duplication.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost was small — about $5-10 million a year for federal water sampling — and the benefit would have been basic, publicly available information about toxic chemicals in drinking water supplies. A nationwide survey does not clean anything up by itself, but it tells communities and regulators where the danger is. There were no significant drawbacks in the bill itself beyond the modest federal expense and possible duplication with state testing, which the bill tried to avoid. The real cost was never learning where the contamination is.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee, then to two of its subcommittees, which held one hearing; the committee never sent it to the floor, and when the Congress ended in January 2021 it was dead.

narrative.text: After introduction on March 28, 2019, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources and never reported out.
In April 2019 it was split between the subcommittees on Energy and Mineral Resources and Water, Oceans, and Wildlife, which together held one hearing on June 13, 2019.
No further action was taken, and the bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that make or use PFAS face no new nationwide map of where their chemicals turned up, and no one — public or industry — gained from the bill's failure; the only winners are whoever preferred the question stay unanswered.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Whoever preferred no contamination map existed

for.name: Rep. Daniel Kildee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited a bipartisan group of cosponsors, including three Republicans.

for.name: 19 of 231 House Democrats and 3 of 197 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan backing from 22 members.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after its single subcommittee hearing; the committee never reported it out or scheduled a vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship — a Michigan Democrat leading with three Republicans among 22 cosponsors — but it was never voted on, so no roll call exists.

industries.industry: PFAS manufacturers and industrial users (chemical makers, makers of nonstick cookware, stain-resistant fabrics, food packaging, firefighting foams)
industries.note: A nationwide map of where these chemicals have ended up would strengthen the record for regulating them, restricting them, and making responsible parties pay for cleanup. It imposes no new rules on them directly, but it builds the evidence base that does.

Utilities that draw from contaminated sources could learn their water contains PFAS, potentially requiring costly treatment or new supply sources. Communities near military and industrial sites with known releases would be tested first.
